'''Neil Hindman''' (born April 14, 1943) is an American [[mathematician]] and professor emeritus<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=People {{!}} Howard University Department of Mathematics |url=https://mathematics.howard.edu/people |access-date=2024-02-25 |website=mathematics.howard.edu}}</ref> at [[Howard University]]. His research focuses on various areas within [[mathematics]], including [[topology]], [[Stone–Čech compactification|Stone-Čech compactification]], [[discrete system]]s, and [[Ramsey theory]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Neil Hindman's Home Page |url=http://nhindman.us/ |access-date=2024-02-25 |website=nhindman.us}}</ref>

== Life and education ==
Neil Hindman actively participated in [[Civil rights movement|civil rights]] work during his college years. In the summer of 1964, he served as a [[Freedom Schools|freedom school]] coordinator in [[Mississippi]].<ref>{{cite podcast|url= https://open.spotify.com/episode/68gxkLOllaD0sA97zQLIOj?si=75caa2c968b344ae|title= The Ramsey Theory Podcast: No Strangers At This Party With Neil Hindman|website= Spotify|publisher=|host= |date= January 5, 2022|time= 14:53|access-date= February 26, 2024}}</ref>

Hindman completed his Bachelor of Arts degree in [[mathematics]] and [[physics]] in 1965 at [[Westmar University|Westmar College]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=Bellringer in the Night |url=https://www.westmarcollege.org/newsletters/200902.pdf |access-date=February 24, 2024 |work=WESTMAR UNIVERSITY ALUMNI AND FRIENDS ASSOCIATION |pages=4}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite web|url=http://nhindman.us/resume.pdf |title=Curriculum vitae|date=September 3, 2025|access-date=2025-09-04}}</ref> He then pursued a graduate degree, earning a Master of Arts in mathematics from the [[University of Massachusetts]] in 1967.<ref name=":1" /> Subsequently, Hindman continued his academic journey at [[Wesleyan University]], where he received his Ph.D. in 1969. Under the supervision of W. W. Comfort, Hindman wrote his doctoral thesis on "P-like spaces and their product with P-spaces.<ref name=":1" />"

== Academic career ==
Neil Hindman began his academic career as a visiting assistant professor at [[Wesleyan University]], serving from September 1969 to June 1970. Following this, he joined [[California State University, Los Angeles]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Retired and Emeriti Faculty {{!}} Cal State LA |url=https://www.calstatela.edu/nss/math/retired-and-emeriti-faculty |access-date=2024-02-25 |website=www.calstatela.edu}}</ref> as an assistant professor in September 1970. From September 1975 to August 1976, Hindman held a visiting associate professorship at [[State University of New York|SUNY]] (The State University of New York) at [[Binghamton, New York|Binghamton]]. By December 1979, he had risen to the rank of Professor at [[California State University, Los Angeles]].

In January 1980, Hindman transitioned to [[Howard University]], where he assumed the role of associate professor, continuing to impart knowledge in [[mathematics]].<ref name=":0" /> He dedicated several decades to teaching and research at [[Howard University]], ultimately retiring as a professor of Mathematics<ref name=":0" /> in June 2017.<ref name=":1" />

== Mathematical work ==
One of Hindman's early contributions was his dissertation for his Ph.D. thesis,<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Comfort |first1=W.W. |last2=Hindman |first2=Neil |last3=Negrepontis |first3=S. |date=March 20, 1968 |title=''F'' <sup>′</sup>-spaces and their product with ''P'' -spaces |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/pacific-journal-of-mathematics/volume-28/issue-3/Fprime-spaces-and-their-product-with-P-spaces/pjm/1102983300.pdf |journal=Pacific Journal of Mathematics |volume=28 |issue=3 |pages=489–502 |doi=10.2140/pjm.1969.28.489 |via=Project Euclid}}</ref> conducted in collaboration with W. W. Comfort and S. Negrepontis. Their research explored conditions for defining F'-spaces and investigated concepts such as weakly Lindelöf spaces and [[P-space]]s, shedding light on the structure of [[F-space]]s in [[topology]]. This pioneering work significantly advanced theoretical models and analytical techniques within the field.

[[IP set|Hindman's Theorem]], formulated and proven by Neil Hindman,<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Hindman |first=Neil |date=October 1, 1972 |title=Finite Sums from Sequences Within Cells of a Partition of N |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82653382.pdf |journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory |volume=A |issue=17 |pages=1–11 |via=CORE}}</ref> addresses a [[conjecture]] originally proposed by [[Ronald Graham|Graham]] and [[Bruce Lee Rothschild|Rothschild]]. The theorem asserts that any partition of the [[natural number]]s <math>\mathbb{N}</math> into a finite number of classes contains at least one class with a [[sequence]] such that all [[finite sum]]s of distinct elements from this [[sequence]] also belong to the same class. [[IP set|Hindman's Theorem]] confirms the [[conjecture]] by [[Ronald Graham|Graham]] and [[Bruce Lee Rothschild|Rothschild]] and establishes its equivalence with the existence of an [[ultrafilter]] on <math>\mathbb{N}</math>. This theorem highlights the relationship between the [[partition regularity]] of the [[natural number]]s and [[ultrafilter]]s, offering a fundamental result with broad implications across various mathematical domains.

Hindman remains active in the fields of [[Ramsey theory|Ramsey Theory]] and [[Topology]], with a particular focus on the [[Stone–Čech compactification]].
